justification: Finding [0] says `canReferenceType` may be missing or the diff incomplete ("If the method is absent, this fails to compile"). The known bug is different: context.ts passes all in-scope pipes rather than only the pipes the template uses. That makes the stricter check force inlining spuriously. The finding never mentions the pipes map being too broad, so it does not match.
ground_truth: `requiresInlineTypeCheckBlock` now requires an inline type-check block whenever any pipe in its `usedPipes` argument cannot be referenced from the TCB environment (`env.canReferenceType`, stricter than the previous "is exported" check). But the caller in context.ts passes `pipes`, the map of all pipes in the component's scope, not just those used in the template. Components that merely have an unreferenceable pipe in scope are now forced to inline, which errors where inlining is unsupported (e.g. the language service reports spurious errors). Fixed by passing only the pipes the template actually uses.

findings.description: The change calls `env.canReferenceType(ref)` and `env.canReferenceType(pipeRef)` on `ReferenceEmitEnvironment`, but the diff does not add that method. It also removes `checkIfClassIsExported` without adding a replacement in the shown files. If the method is absent, this fails to compile. If it is added elsewhere, the diff is incomplete and the exported check cannot be verified. The new test also passes a `{rootDir: '/root'}` option to `diagnose`, and that signature change is not shown either.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says the guard uses the generic `_placeholderRe`, which SafeSelector also uses for attribute selectors, so a part containing an attribute placeholder followed by a hex char gets the separator skipped. It also says the check doesn't verify the separator is a space. That covers the `:host[foo]>div` case. Its suggested fix of only matching escape-specific placeholders is the actual fix.
ground_truth: To avoid treating the space in an escaped selector (".\fc ber") as a combinator, the PR skips a separator when the preceding part matches `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`) and the next character is a hex digit. But SafeSelector uses the same `__ph-N__` placeholder for attribute selectors and other content, not only for escape sequences. In minified CSS without spaces, e.g. `:host[foo]>div`, the `>` separator is skipped because the part contains an attribute placeholder and the next char 'd' is hex, so the selector is scoped incorrectly and styles on :host attributes break in production builds. Fixed by giving escapes their own `__esc-ph-N__` placeholder and checking only for that.

findings.description: The new guard uses the generic `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`), but SafeSelector uses that placeholder for attribute selectors (`[attr=...]`) and `:not(...)` content as well as for escapes. A selector like `a[href] big` or `[type=text] div` therefore has a part ending in a placeholder. If the next character is a hex digit or letter a-f (`b`, `d`, `a`, ...), the descendant-combinator space is treated as part of an escape and skipped. The two compound selectors are then merged and scoped once, so output like `a[href] big[contenta]` is wrong. This is a regression for ordinary selectors. The check should only match placeholders created for backslash escapes. The check also does not verify that the separator is a space, so `.\fc>b` is wrongly skipped too.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same mechanism: the check `part.match(_placeholderRe)` matches attribute-selector placeholders as well as escapes. When the next char is hex, the separator is wrongly skipped and scoping breaks. Its example uses a descendant space ("[type=text] div") rather than the minified `>` case, but the defect is the same. Its suggested fix, distinguishing escape placeholders, mirrors the actual fix.
ground_truth: To avoid treating the space in an escaped selector (".\fc ber") as a combinator, the PR skips a separator when the preceding part matches `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`) and the next character is a hex digit. But SafeSelector uses the same `__ph-N__` placeholder for attribute selectors and other content, not only for escape sequences. In minified CSS without spaces, e.g. `:host[foo]>div`, the `>` separator is skipped because the part contains an attribute placeholder and the next char 'd' is hex, so the selector is scoped incorrectly and styles on :host attributes break in production builds. Fixed by giving escapes their own `__esc-ph-N__` placeholder and checking only for that.

findings.description: The new check treats any part containing a `__ph-N__` placeholder as an escaped hex value. SafeSelector also uses placeholders for attribute selectors (`[attr]`) and `:nth-*(...)` expressions. For a selector such as `[type=text] div`, `a[href] b`, `.x[data-y] a` or `:nth-child(2) em`, the part contains a placeholder and the next character is a hex char (a-f or a digit). The code then skips the descendant-combinator split and the selectors are no longer scoped separately. `[type=text] div` loses the scoping on `div`, and the output has the wrong shape. This regresses scoping for common selectors. The check should confirm that the placeholder is an escape ending in a hex sequence, not merely a placeholder that appears in the part.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the removal of the `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards in test_hooks.ts. It says that loading the module outside a test framework will throw `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. That is the same faulty code and failure mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: While replacing `global` with `globalThis`, the PR removed the guards around the Jasmine/Jest hooks in `@angular/core/testing` test_hooks.ts: `if (_global.beforeEach) {...}` became an unconditional `beforeEach(...)` / `afterEach(...)`. When this module is evaluated outside a test runner (e.g. it ends up in an application bundle), `beforeEach` is undefined and loading the module throws a ReferenceError. Fixed by calling `globalThis.beforeEach?.(...)` / `globalThis.afterEach?.(...)`.

findings.description: The `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` now run unconditionally when the module loads. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework has defined these globals (a server bundle, a Node script, a non-Jasmine/Mocha/Jest runner), loading the module throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. The old code tolerated this case. A `typeof beforeEach === 'function'` guard is needed.

justification: Finding [0] matches the known bug. It points at the same change in test_hooks.ts, the removal of the `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards. It also gives the same failure mechanism: "If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework has defined these globals... the import throws a `ReferenceError`".
ground_truth: While replacing `global` with `globalThis`, the PR removed the guards around the Jasmine/Jest hooks in `@angular/core/testing` test_hooks.ts: `if (_global.beforeEach) {...}` became an unconditional `beforeEach(...)` / `afterEach(...)`. When this module is evaluated outside a test runner (e.g. it ends up in an application bundle), `beforeEach` is undefined and loading the module throws a ReferenceError. Fixed by calling `globalThis.beforeEach?.(...)` / `globalThis.afterEach?.(...)`.

findings.description: The previous `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework has defined these globals, such as a non-test context or a runner that does not expose them, the import throws a `ReferenceError`. Before this change it was a silent no-op.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It says that in `collectDeferredSymbols`, "`deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` is never set" and keeps its initial `false`. As a result, the defer deps functions emit `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m => m.default`, so the dynamic import resolves to undefined. That is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: The PR adds support for default imports in `@defer` dependencies and records `isDefaultImport` in the `deferrableTypes` map, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects (they keep the initial `isDefaultImport: false`). The generated dependency loader function for the defer block reads that flag, so for a default-imported component it emits `m.ComponentName` instead of `m.default`, and loading the deferred block yields undefined. Fixed by setting `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)` in `collectDeferredSymbols`.

findings.description: In `collectDeferredSymbols`, `deferBlockDep.isDeferrable` and `importPath` are updated, but `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` is never set. It stays at its initial `false` from `resolve`. The defer deps functions in `template.ts`, `create_defer_deps_fns.ts` and `compiler.ts` read `dep.isDefaultImport` from the defer block dependency. For a default-imported component they therefore still emit `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m => m.default`, so the dynamic import resolves to `undefined` at runtime. Only the `deferrableTypes` map, used for `setClassMetadataAsync`, gets the correct flag. The new tests that expect `m.default` in the `TestCmp_Defer_1_DepsFn` would fail.

justification: The known bug is that `collectDeferredSymbols` never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport`, so per-block deps keep the initial `false` and the loader emits `m.Name` instead of `m.default`. Finding [0] describes a different defect: `isDefaultImport()` misclassifies mixed imports such as `import Foo, {Bar}`. It does not mention the missing assignment on the per-block dependency objects.
ground_truth: The PR adds support for default imports in `@defer` dependencies and records `isDefaultImport` in the `deferrableTypes` map, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects (they keep the initial `isDefaultImport: false`). The generated dependency loader function for the defer block reads that flag, so for a default-imported component it emits `m.ComponentName` instead of `m.default`, and loading the deferred block yields undefined. Fixed by setting `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)` in `collectDeferredSymbols`.

findings.description: isDefaultImport() only returns true when the import clause has no namedBindings. A mixed import such as `import Foo, {Bar} from './x'` has namedBindings, so it is treated as not default. If the default-imported `Foo` is used in a `@defer` block or in `deferredImports`, the generated loader is `m => m.Foo` instead of `m => m.default`. That resolves to undefined at runtime. The check also does not look at which binding is being deferred, only at the declaration's shape.

justification: Finding 0 is about the inverted `!isAnchorElement` check in the constructor and the resulting loss of the default `tabindex=0` on non-anchor hosts. That is a different defect from relative-link hrefs going stale. Finding 1 says the default-handling clause is negated and that the link "subscribes when nothing depends on router state." This is exactly the excluded interpretation: its fix would subscribe in fewer cases. It never identifies that relative links depend on the ActivatedRoute and so always need the subscription.
ground_truth: RouterLink on anchor elements now only subscribes to router NavigationEnd events (to recompute `href`) when `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` decides the link depends on router state, i.e. only for `preserveFragment` or `queryParamsHandling` 'merge'/'preserve' (plus a clause about the router's default handling). But the href of a relative link also changes whenever navigation changes the ActivatedRoute it resolves against. E.g. `<a [routerLink]="['./child']" queryParamsHandling="replace">` keeps showing `/initial/child` after navigating to `/different`. The optimization's premise is wrong, so hrefs go stale after navigation. The fix removes the condition and always subscribes for anchor elements (effectively rolling back the PR). A finding that only says the default-handling clause is inverted, and implies subscribing in fewer cases, is a different defect: its fix would remove subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix.

findings.description: The constructor condition is inverted. Previously anchor elements subscribed to navigation events and non-anchor elements got `tabindex=0`. Now `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary()` runs only when `!isAnchorElement`, where it returns immediately. The `else` branch calls `setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0')` only for anchor elements, where it is a no-op. As a result, non-anchor hosts such as `<div routerLink>` never get the default `tabindex="0"`, so they are no longer keyboard-focusable. That is an accessibility and behavior regression.

The subscription condition looks wrong. When no `queryParamsHandling` is set and the router's default is `merge` or `preserve`, `createSubcription` stays false, so the link never subscribes to `NavigationEnd`. Its href then goes stale after navigation, because the generated URL depends on the current router state. Conversely, it subscribes when nothing depends on router state. The logic is negated.

justification: Neither finding identifies the actual defect: anchor links must always subscribe to NavigationEnd, because relative links resolve against the ActivatedRoute and their href changes after navigation. Finding 0 is about the inverted `if (!this.isAnchorElement)` in the constructor and the resulting loss of tabindex on non-anchor hosts, which is a different issue. Finding 1 says the default-handling clause is inverted and proposes removing the negation. That is exactly the excluded case: in the default config the change would drop subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix. It never says the optimization's premise (only router-state-dependent links need updates) is wrong.
ground_truth: RouterLink on anchor elements now only subscribes to router NavigationEnd events (to recompute `href`) when `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` decides the link depends on router state, i.e. only for `preserveFragment` or `queryParamsHandling` 'merge'/'preserve' (plus a clause about the router's default handling). But the href of a relative link also changes whenever navigation changes the ActivatedRoute it resolves against. E.g. `<a [routerLink]="['./child']" queryParamsHandling="replace">` keeps showing `/initial/child` after navigating to `/different`. The optimization's premise is wrong, so hrefs go stale after navigation. The fix removes the condition and always subscribes for anchor elements (effectively rolling back the PR). A finding that only says the default-handling clause is inverted, and implies subscribing in fewer cases, is a different defect: its fix would remove subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix.

findings.description: The constructor condition is inverted: `if (!this.isAnchorElement) { this.subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary(); } else { this.setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0'); }`. `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` returns early for non-anchor elements, so that call does nothing. The `tabindex="0"` fallback now runs only for anchor elements. Non-anchor hosts such as `<div routerLink>` no longer get a default tabindex and lose keyboard focusability, which is a regression. The condition should be `if (this.isAnchorElement)`.

The subscription condition for the router-state dependency is wrong. It subscribes when `!queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(options.defaultQueryParamsHandling)`, meaning when no handling applies, and it skips subscribing when the global default is 'merge' or 'preserve'. With `defaultQueryParamsHandling: 'merge'` and no per-link handling, the href depends on current router state but never updates on NavigationEnd, so it goes stale. The negation on the default should be removed.

justification: Finding 0 names the same mechanism as the known bug. It says the change from `toPromise()` to `first()` makes empty-completing sources reject with EmptyError instead of resolving `undefined`, so "navigation fail[s] with `EmptyError`". It applies this to canLoad guards and loadChildren in recognize. That is the same defect, even though it does not mention matchWithChecks or the NoMatch catch.
ground_truth: The PR replaces `.toPromise()` with a custom `firstValueFrom` (built on rxjs `first()`) in route recognition (`matchWithChecks`, `runCanLoadGuards`, `loadChildren`). Unlike `toPromise()`, which resolves `undefined` when an observable completes without emitting, `first()` errors with an EmptyError. Guards or matchers whose observables complete without emitting now throw EmptyError instead of being treated as "no match"; the recognizer's catch only skips NoMatch errors, so navigation fails instead of moving on to the next route. Fixed by also treating EmptyError as a non-match in recognize.ts.

findings.description: The replacement is not equivalent to the old `.toPromise()`. `toPromise()` resolved `undefined` when the source completed without emitting, and it used the last emitted value. `first()` instead rejects with `EmptyError` on an empty-completing source and takes the first value. A `redirectTo` function, `canLoad` guard, or `loadChildren` observable that completes empty used to resolve to `undefined` and now makes navigation fail with `EmptyError`. For `loadChildren`, that bypasses the `if (!cfg) throw canLoadFails(route)` handling.

justification: Finding 0 describes the known bug. It notes that the TNode is shared across instances, so cancelLeavingNodes force-cancels and removes an unrelated instance's leaving element whenever that element sits in a different parent: "The different-parent heuristic cannot tell an overlay re-creation from an unrelated instance, so it breaks leave animations for unrelated elements." Findings 1 and 2 describe different issues: memory and leak tracking in 1, and stray enter animations in 2.
ground_truth: `cancelLeavingNodes` now force-removes any element tracked as leaving for the same TNode whenever it sits in a different DOM parent than the newly inserted element (added to de-duplicate dynamic components re-rendered into a fresh overlay pane). `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, which is shared by every instance of a template, so distinct sibling instances (e.g. an accordion where opening section B collapses section A in another parent) are also "different parent": the still-animating element is removed synchronously and its `animate.leave` animation is skipped. Fixed by tracking the declaration view of each leaving element and only doing the cross-parent removal for the same logical view.

findings.description: cancelLeavingNodes cancels any leaving element for the same tNode whose parent differs from the new element's parent. A tNode belongs to the TView, so every instance of a component or template shares it. If instance A's element is playing its leave animation and instance B is inserted into a different parent (for example, two sibling components or list items each with an `animate.leave` element), A's animation is cut short. A's element receives a synthetic cancel `animationend` and is removed from the DOM immediately. The different-parent heuristic cannot tell an overlay re-creation from an unrelated instance, so it breaks leave animations for unrelated elements.

On Detach, the element is now tracked in leavingNodes whenever the tNode has leave animations. That happens even when runLeaveAnimationsWithCallback skips the animation and removes the node immediately, for example when animations are disabled or the element has no actual animation. The entries are only cleared by the leave-animation cleanup, so they can stay in the array indefinitely. The array then holds references to detached DOM elements and grows with each detach. The tracking also runs for every detached node that has leave data, which adds work to a hot path.

The removal of pending enter animations from the queue was dropped when a node with an enter animation is detached. If an element is created and removed before the animation queue flushes, its enter animation function still runs against a node that has already been removed or is leaving. This can start a stray enter animation, or add classes and listeners to the leaving element and interfere with the leave animation.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It says the TNode is shared across instances and that `cancelLeavingNodes` "cancels any leaving element whose parent differs from the new element's parent". As a result, unrelated instances' leave animations are "forcibly cancelled and its element removed early". This is the same mechanism as the known bug, which the fix addresses by tracking the declaration view. Findings 1 and 2 describe different issues: stale tracking entries leaking, and dropped enter-animation queue removal.
ground_truth: `cancelLeavingNodes` now force-removes any element tracked as leaving for the same TNode whenever it sits in a different DOM parent than the newly inserted element (added to de-duplicate dynamic components re-rendered into a fresh overlay pane). `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, which is shared by every instance of a template, so distinct sibling instances (e.g. an accordion where opening section B collapses section A in another parent) are also "different parent": the still-animating element is removed synchronously and its `animate.leave` animation is skipped. Fixed by tracking the declaration view of each leaving element and only doing the cross-parent removal for the same logical view.

findings.description: A TNode is shared by every instance of a template or component, but `cancelLeavingNodes` cancels any leaving element whose parent differs from the new element's parent. For example, two instances of a component each contain `@if (x) { <div animate.leave> }`. Instance 1's div is animating out in parent P1, and instance 2 then inserts the same TNode in parent P2. Instance 1's leave animation is forcibly cancelled and its element removed early, although the two are unrelated. The same happens for `@for` over components or for a template rendered in different containers. This is a regression: leave animations are skipped incorrectly whenever the same TNode is used in different parents.

`trackLeavingNodes` is called on every Detach of a node that has a leave animation, but nothing guarantees `clearLeavingNodes` runs afterwards. This applies when animations are disabled, when the leave function is skipped, or when the leaving node is a descendant that is removed together with its parent. The element then stays in the `leavingNodes` array for that TNode, which leaks DOM nodes. A later insert of the same TNode can also wrongly match a stale element and cancel or remove it.

The removal of queued enter animations for a node that is being detached was dropped, as was the `cancelLeavingNodes` call in the animate instructions. If an element is created and removed before the animation queue flushes, as with rapid toggling, its pending enter animation is no longer discarded. It then runs against a detached or leaving element, which can add stray enter classes or fire listeners and leave state inconsistent.

justification: Both findings describe the same defect as the known bug: the wire format changed from a comma-separated string to a JSON array string, and the backend consumer was not updated. Finding 0 makes this point for findConstructorByPosition: "now yields the string literal \"[0,1,2]\"... receiving `findConstructorByPosition` does not appear to be updated... would fail". Finding 1 makes the same point for findDomElementByPosition.
ground_truth: To escape code injected into the inspected page, the PR changes `findConstructorByPosition('${position}')` and `findDomElementByPosition('${position}')` to pass `stringifyAndEscape(position)`. `position` is an array, so it used to be serialized implicitly as a comma-separated string ("0,1,2"); now it is passed as a JSON array string ("[0,1,2]"). The backend that parses this serialized id still expects the comma-separated format, so "view source" and "select DOM element" from the component tree break. The fix updates the backend (component-tree.ts) to the new format; the PR changed the wire format without updating its consumer.

findings.description: `position` is an `ElementPosition` (number[]). The old template literal turned it into a comma-separated string such as '0,1,2'. `stringifyAndEscape` now yields the string literal "[0,1,2]", including brackets. The receiving `findConstructorByPosition` does not appear to be updated in this diff; it most likely still parses with `split(',').map(parseInt)`. That would produce NaN for the first and last indices, so View Source would fail to resolve the element or throw.

The same change affects `findDomElementByPosition`. It now receives the string "[0,1,2]" instead of '0,1,2'. If the receiver still splits on commas, the indices are parsed as NaN, so selecting a DOM element from the component tree breaks.

justification: Finding 0 explains that `position` used to be serialized via toString into the comma-separated "0,1,2" and is now sent as the JSON string "[0,1,2]". It says the receiving side, which parses with split(','), was not updated, so view source breaks. It notes the same problem in findDomElementByPosition. This is exactly the known bug.
ground_truth: To escape code injected into the inspected page, the PR changes `findConstructorByPosition('${position}')` and `findDomElementByPosition('${position}')` to pass `stringifyAndEscape(position)`. `position` is an array, so it used to be serialized implicitly as a comma-separated string ("0,1,2"); now it is passed as a JSON array string ("[0,1,2]"). The backend that parses this serialized id still expects the comma-separated format, so "view source" and "select DOM element" from the component tree break. The fix updates the backend (component-tree.ts) to the new format; the PR changed the wire format without updating its consumer.

findings.description: The serialization of `position` changed. Before, `'${position}'` interpolated the array via toString, so the inspected app received a comma-separated string like "0,1,2". Now `stringifyAndEscape(position)` passes the string "[0,1,2]". If `findConstructorByPosition` still parses its input with `split(',')` and `parseInt`, the first and last indices become NaN ("[0" and "2]"). The element lookup then fails and view-source stops working. The receiving side is not updated in this diff. The same applies to `findDomElementByPosition` in `selectDomElement`.
